International Business Machines (IBM) has just completed a CAD 997.11 million fixed income offering of 4.750% notes due August 15, 2034. This provides investors with fresh information on the company's funding costs and capital structure.

The bond issuance comes as International Business Machines shares trade at US$236.31, with the 7 day share price return up 4.42% but the 30 day share price return down 17.82%. The 5 year total shareholder return of 108.63% points to stronger longer term compounding.

If the recent funding move has you thinking more broadly about opportunities in AI infrastructure, this can be a good moment to scan 56 AI infrastructure stocks.

After a sharp pullback from recent highs, yet with International Business Machines still supported by fresh bond market access and a long dividend record, are you looking at a lot of the upside already realized, or is meaningful value still on the table?

Most Popular Narrative: 7.7% Undervalued

The most followed narrative on International Business Machines currently anchors fair value at $256.08 versus the last close at $236.31, which frames the recent bond issue against a stock that this narrative views as undervalued.

IBM represents a defensive growth technology investment transitioning into a software and AI-led enterprise platform company. While topline growth remains moderate, improving mix (software), strong margins, and durable cash flows underpin a compelling long-term investment case, particularly for investors seeking exposure to enterprise AI with lower volatility than pure-play SaaS peers.

Want to see how that fair value for International Business Machines is built? The narrative focuses on steady revenue growth, expanding margins, and a future earnings multiple that assumes IBM is treated more like a compounder than a slow legacy stock.

According to kapirey, this most popular narrative applies a 9.55% discount rate, assumes revenue and profit margins that reflect IBM's push toward higher margin software and AI, and arrives at a fair value of $256.08, which is 7.7% above the current share price. It considers the recent earnings trajectory, cash generation, and business mix shift as key inputs to justify a higher valuation anchor than where the market is currently pricing the stock.

title: Palantir's Sovereign AI Boom Is Almost Entirely In America
detail:
Palantir's Sovereign AI Boom Is Almost Entirely In America
Trefis Team
Tue, August 11, 2026 at 6:23 AM PDT 3 min read
PLTR
^GSPC
MSFT
GOOG
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by athree23 on Pixabay

The quarter that repriced the stock was made overwhelmingly at home, and the segment lines say so.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock gained 39.5% in the week after its second-quarter report, climbing from $125.65 to $175.23 while the S&P 500 added 2.0%. The quarter was a record on almost every line. But a move that size is a bet on the forward number rather than the reported one, and Palantir's raised forward number rests almost entirely on one country.

A Record Quarter And An Even Bigger Guide

Second-quarter revenue grew 93% year over year to $1.935 billion, the fastest rate Palantir has ever reported. A record growth rate is history by the time it prints. The guide is: management lifting its full-year 2026 revenue guidance midpoint to $8.154 billion, 82% growth and an 11-point increase on the prior full-year guide, the largest raise it has ever made. Adding eleven points of annual growth in one reporting cycle is what re-prices a stock, and the tape says this was specific to Palantir, with MSFT up 3.8% and GOOGL down 4.3% over the same week.

Over 81% Of Revenue Now Comes From America

The U.S. business now makes up over 81% of revenue and grew 115%, with U.S. commercial revenue up 149% to $764 million and U.S. government revenue up 90%. Commercial demand elsewhere is a different story: international commercial revenue reached $182 million, up 26% from a year earlier but only 2% from the prior three months.

The pitch behind the U.S. surge is AI sovereignty, data analytics software that leaves customers holding their own data, logic, and model weights instead of handing them to an outside lab. Management frames that as something America and the West need, yet the CEO concedes the growth Palantir gets from the European institutions it keeps serving is poor.

Palantir's government work now runs deeper than software: adjusted gross margin was held to 86% partly because it took on cloud hosting for one of its government customers, a cost a pure software vendor would not normally carry.

Returns that lean this heavily on one theme in one market are a different kind of exposure, and the Trefis High Quality Portfolio does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.

The Next Raise Is The Load-Bearing Number

At $175.23 the stock is still about 15% below its 52-week high of $207.18, so even a move this size only recovered ground. Because the guide did the repricing, the guide is what has to keep moving: the company now guides to U.S. commercial growth of at least 134% for full year 2026, and $13.1 billion of total remaining deal value still has to convert into revenue. The counterweight, on the government side at least, is management's own headroom argument: Palantir's Department of War revenue over the trailing twelve months is under 0.25% of the Pentagon's budget, so the domestic engine has room to keep running. Whether the raises keep arriving is the test, so the companies whose forward guidance keeps climbing are worth tracking as a group.

title: ACN: Priced Like A Decline, Paying Like A Machine

ACN: Priced Like A Decline, Paying Like A Machine
Trefis Team

Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The market has punished this consulting giant as if its business model is failing, yet the company's cash machine continues to run smoothly.

The market's verdict on Accenture (ACN) is written in its stock chart. Trading at about $175.72 a share, IT consulting firm is 54% below its two-year high. A fall that deep implies a business in serious trouble. Yet the company's cash statement tells a different story, generating 11.7% of its market value in free cash per year. Is this business actually broken, or just violently marked down?

The cash statement tells a story of stability.

Accenture's core business is helping large enterprises manage technology and operations, a model that produces consistent results. The company's free cash flow yield of 11.7% is nearly triple the 4.2% S&P 500 median. This isn't a one-time event; its three-year average operating margin is a steady 15.6%, close to its current trailing margin of 15.8%.

Even as the stock price fell, the top line kept expanding, with revenue over the last twelve months growing 6.7%. The company is still winning large contracts, landing 104 client bookings over $100 million in the first nine months of its fiscal year, an increase from the prior year. This suggests deep client relationships remain intact, funding the cash flow that contradicts the stock price.

The market is pricing in specific, near-term damage.

The selloff isn't baseless. On its latest earnings call, management detailed new challenges that spooked investors. The company saw a revenue impact of approximately $100 million from the conflict in the Middle East, which hit discretionary, consulting type of work. More concerning was the news that "a couple of our large managed services opportunities moved into FY 2027 for company-specific reasons."

These are not small issues. Large managed services contracts provide a predictable, recurring revenue base. Pushing them out creates an unexpected gap. This uncertainty is why management warned that for the upcoming fourth quarter, more of the guided range is in play. The market's fear is that these problems are not isolated incidents, but the first signs of a broader slowdown in corporate spending. A recent analysis explores the turbulence priced into the stock, examining the pressures that have weighed on investor sentiment.

The fourth-quarter revenue result is the first real test.

The contrarian argument for Accenture hinges on the durability of its cash generation. The market has already priced in the recent bad news. The question now is whether the business can execute against these lowered expectations, proving the recent pressures are manageable rather than systemic.

The useful question for a holder is not which way this breaks, but how much of the position the priced band puts in play.

International Business Machines (IBM) trades at about $237.28, and its option chain prices a band running from $155 to $358.42 over the next ten months or so. That band is not a forecast. It measures the room a holder is carrying, and the useful work is turning it into money rather than into a view on direction. The stock already sits about 28% below its 52-week high.

The $155 Floor And The $358 Ceiling In Your Own Money

From today's price the ceiling sits about 51% higher and the floor about 35% lower. On a $10,000 position that band is about $5,110 of gain or $3,470 of loss, with roughly two chances in three of finishing between them. The wider upside is not a market view: a band like this always runs further above than below, because a stock can fall only to zero but rise without limit. While both ends of the band stretch beyond anything the stock has traded in the past year, the floor is the more extreme departure: with a trailing 52-week low of $199.19, the downside plunges much further past recent support than the ceiling pushes past recent highs, and a fall that far takes a much larger gain to undo than to cause. That asymmetry is the arithmetic the Trefis High Quality Portfolio is built around.

Options Are Pricing Less Movement Than IBM Has Actually Delivered

The implied volatility behind that band, 44%, runs below the 48% the stock has actually moved over the trailing year. That gap is unusual: the market expects calmer action than IBM has recently produced. That is not the same as cheap, since a broad reading of IBM implied volatility still sits in the 78th percentile of its own trailing one-year range. The premiums share the band's structural asymmetry, but they lean protective: while traders are paying 1.4 times as much in dollar terms for upside calls as for downside puts, that ratio sits well below the mechanical baseline, meaning downside protection is actually catching a relative bid.

The June Quarter The Band Is Still Arguing About

A band that wide is an unanswered question with a price on it. In the June quarter tens of large deals failed to close on the timelines the company expected, and that slippage was most of the reason the quarter fell short of expectations. Those deals ride on enterprise license agreements bundled with the mainframe and bought as capital spending, so when clients redirected money toward servers, storage and memory ahead of expected price increases, transaction processing revenue fell 9%. Management lowered its full-year revenue growth range to 4% to 5% in constant currency, from 5%-plus in April. Its best indication so far that the demand was deferred rather than destroyed is that about a third of the slipped deals closed within three weeks of the quarter ending, against the two-thirds to three-quarters normally expected over six months.

IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Shares of Monday.com (NASDAQ: MNDY) rose 20.4% in July 2026, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The workflow-automation specialist mainly followed broad growth-stock vibes up and down, but sprinted ahead in the last few days of the month thanks to a radical corporate restructuring.

A volatile month in three acts

Monday.com's July journey had three distinct legs:

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The stock posted a 20% gain from June 30 to July 13. Monday.com had no market-moving news of its own in this period. Instead, the volatile stock amplified a market rotation into enterprise software investments.

On July 14, IBM (NYSE: IBM) sparked another round of Street skepticism in the software sector with a weak preliminary earnings report. Big Blue said that data center construction is taking budgets away from software sales these days, and that's bad news for app development and project management experts such as Monday.com. A 25% price drop followed over the next week, erasing the gains of early July.

The market narrative started to turn as the Magnificent 7 companies reported earnings between July 22 and July 29. IBM's data center warning proved real, but the hyperscalers still reported strong software and services results. Monday.com accelerated its rebound by announcing a deep restructuring on July 22, and investors applauded the marginwidening effects of a 20% workforce reduction. Though tucked away in an SEC filing, the announcement helped Monday.com climb the same 20% hill it had crested earlier in the month.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
What July (and early August) means for investors

The resulting July jump deserves some additional context. Monday.com reported Q2 2026 results in the early morning hours of Aug. 10, exceeding analyst estimates across the board while reaffirming the guidance it offered alongside the restructuring.

The stock opened 11% lower on the news, removing some of last month's gains. I called Monday.com "volatile" earlier, and I meant it.

In the report, co-founders and co-CEOs Roy Mann and Eran Zinman said that Monday.com's strategy is working well. The restructuring wasn't meant to fix a broken business plan, but to "capture the largest opportunity we have ever seen in software" with a leaner and more effective workforce.

title: Silicon Motion Rides on Solid Revenue Growth: Time to Buy the Stock?
detail:
Silicon Motion Rides on Solid Revenue Growth: Time to Buy the Stock?
Supriyo Bose

SIMO
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Silicon Motion Technology Corporation SIMO is benefiting from strong momentum across its storage-controller portfolio, driven by market-share gains, new product ramps and growing exposure to enterprise and artificial intelligence (AI)-related storage applications.

The company's rapidly expanding embedded storage business, strength in SSD controllers and increasing contribution from enterprise and automotive storage solutions are driving robust top-line growth. These factors position Silicon Motion well to sustain its growth trajectory through the remainder of 2026.

Robust Revenue Growth Bodes Well for SIMO

Silicon Motion delivered an impressive second quarter, with revenues surging 127% year over year and 32% sequentially to $451 million. The performance also exceeded the company's earlier guidance of $393-$411 million, highlighting stronger-than-anticipated demand across its portfolio.

The momentum was broad-based. SSD controller sales increased 50-55% year over year and 5-10% sequentially. eMMC+UFS controller sales jumped 95-100% from the year-ago quarter and 15-20% sequentially. Sales from Ferri and Boot Drive solutions soared 1,690-1,695% year over year and 110-115% sequentially.

The strong performance follows an equally encouraging first quarter, when revenues surged 105% year over year and 23% sequentially to $342.1 million. The sustained acceleration underscores Silicon Motion's success in expanding its addressable market beyond its traditional consumer NAND flash controller business.

Zacks Investment Research


Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

SIMO's Growth Momentum Set to Continue

Management expects the strong top-line trajectory to continue in the third quarter of 2026. Silicon Motion projects revenues between $519 million and $541 million, indicating sequential growth of 15-20% and year-over-year growth of 114-124%.

At the midpoint of $530 million, the guidance represents another significant step up from second-quarter revenues of $451 million and first-quarter revenues of $342.1 million. The trend suggests that Silicon Motion is not merely benefiting from a favorable comparison with the prior year but is generating substantial sequential expansion as new products and customer programs ramp.

Growth is being supported by several catalysts. The company is expanding its presence in embedded eMMC and UFS controllers, while its 6nm PCIe Gen 5 SSD controller portfolio strengthens its position in higher-performance storage applications. Silicon Motion is also targeting enterprise and AI infrastructure opportunities through its MonTitan enterprise SSD controllers and Enterprise Boot Drive solutions.

The MonTitan platform, in particular, expands Silicon Motion's addressable market beyond its historically consumer-focused business. Earlier this year, management observed that two customers were already in production and five additional major cloud-service-provider customers were expected to ramp in the latter half.

Incorporated in 1911, International Business Machines, or IBM, is one of the oldest technology companies in the world. It provides software, IT consulting services, and hardware to help business customers modernize their technology workflows. IBM operates in 175 countries and employs approximately 300,000 people. The company has a robust roster of business partners to service its clients, which includes 95% of all Fortune 500 companies. IBM's products, including Red Hat, watsonx, and mainframes, handle some of the world's most important data workloads in areas like finance and retail. This diversified revenue base provides a stable foundation for its shareholder return policies.

International Business Machines Corp's Dividend Analysis · us.finance.gurufocus
A Glimpse at International Business Machines Corp's Dividend History

International Business Machines Corp has maintained a consistent dividend payment record since 1986. Dividends are currently distributed on a quarterly basis, providing a regular income stream to investors. The company has increased its dividend each year since 1994, earning the prestigious title of a "dividend aristocrat"an honor given to companies that have increased their dividend each year for at least the past 32 years. This long track record demonstrates management's commitment to returning capital to shareholders even through various economic cycles.
